compare_blocks.title: The key difference

compare_blocks.body:
The premise is aligned conditions: the same equipment, the same records, the same authority and deadline. If one is the shift owner and the other merely passing by, duty will cover both columns, with no relation to type.

Each row gives the same scene, the same information and the same constraints, states the basis each may attend to, and notes which axis it illustrates. Both types can use the other's approach; the table records only which is taken first more often, not who is right.

| The same scene (one set of information, the same constraints) | ESTP: the basis more likely attended to | INFP: the basis more likely attended to | What this row illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A noise record arrives | Whether readings, timestamps and the last service line up, and which items are confirmed | Why the accounts differ, and whether the same clue repeats across shifts | Sourcing preference, leaning S/N |

compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
Only P is shared. E/I, S/N and T/F each describes a separate difference.

The shared P is easily read as "neither likes being managed by process", which mistakes outward stance for discipline. P says only that, facing the outer world, both more often take information in and leave room to adjust; how an inspection sheet is filled, how a shift is handed over, how detailed a record is — those follow the post and the procedure, and either type can be strict about them. If the resemblance stops at "neither follows process", every later comparison is bent out of shape.

The differences are read on all three axes at once: whether sourcing trusts checkable facts and past experience, or notices connections and possibility faster; whether the weighing relies on criteria that can be applied consistently, or counts people and costs in; and whether attention turns outward to the floor or inward for a first pass of one's own. All three coexist; the difference is which is relied on more often.

### Gearbox noise on the night shift: the same information, two weighings

In this fictional night-shift example, two workers hear the same unusual gearbox noise and have access to the same records. They have the same reporting duty and authority. Abnormal equipment noise is an abnormal condition: report it under site procedure first, and let qualified, authorised people decide from the equipment documentation and the procedure whether it can keep running — that applies to both, and neither may decide from a type to open the unit or relax a condition. What follows looks only at which information each may attend to, and how the basis is stated.

One approach emphasises confirmed observations in the existing records, such as the time the sound was heard and the last service date. That illustrates Sensing. Separately, asking whether the same reporting criterion applies across comparable shifts illustrates Thinking.

Another approach looks for a pattern across the same shift records or considers more than one explanation for what was reported. That illustrates Intuition. Separately, weighing how the handover affects the next crew illustrates Feeling. Either worker could use all four perspectives without changing the reporting procedure.

The costs sit on either side. Someone whose attention goes to the readings faster may underestimate communication lag: the information is still in one person's hands while others carry on the old way. Someone whose attention goes to people earlier may be caught by "who will be blamed" before the equipment state is clear, and the report may omit a detail that the next shift needs. Neither cost is about preference; both depend on the information, duty and deadline of the moment.

Keep the counterexamples. ESTP will open the documentation and call a qualified person when the equipment is unfamiliar; INFP will shout stop and report the moment someone moves toward a running part. The fork is not who moves first but which kind of basis is cited more often from the same information; sequence is not a criterion.

### Why not one function name overlaps

In the four-function notation used here, ESTP is Se–Ti–Fe–Ni and INFP is Fi–Ne–Si–Te. Side by side nothing shares a name: on the perceiving side Se and Ni against Ne and Si; on the judging side Ti and Fe against Fi and Te.

More precisely, the two share no function with the same name and attitude; each has perceiving and judging processes, but the processes in the dominant and auxiliary positions, and their directions, differ. ESTP's dominant faces outward and stays close to the facts at hand; INFP's dominant faces inward and stays close to the values they hold. That does not mean one has more or fewer mental operations than the other.

Function positions are the model's description of preference; they cannot be read as a sequence of actions, and they are not a list of strengths. Using them to infer whether two people work well together, or who attracts whom, goes beyond what this writing can support.

The attitude of the third position is not consistent across tables: for ESTP's Fe and INFP's Si, some writings mark an explicit attitude and some give only the function name. The disagreement does not change the first two positions; when reading a stack, check which set it declares. Both base descriptions are the [ESTP profile](/en/personality/estp) and the [INFP profile](/en/personality/infp).
compare_blocks.title: Why they are easily confused

compare_blocks.body:
Scope note: the three passages below are editorial fictions about ordinary situations, covering the organisation of information and communication only, not equipment handling procedure. Noise, temperature, vibration and fitness to continue running are equipment and safety judgements, decided by qualified, authorised people under the equipment documentation and site procedure; what the two can do is state clearly what they saw and heard, report through the process, and make the handover and the human impact clear. In an emergency, seek help first and act on site and professional guidance.

### After the noise: who sets the threshold, how communication is arranged

(Fictional scene.) The threshold is not set by a type. Temperature limits, vibration limits and the permitted ways to run come from the manufacturer's documentation and site procedure, signed off by qualified and authorised people. When neither is in that role, what they can do is record the symptom, the timestamp and the report already made, and mark clearly in the handover what has no conclusion yet.

On that basis, each may watch a different stretch. ESTP more often watches whether the criterion is applied consistently: is this the same standard as last time, has anyone relaxed it on experience. INFP more often watches how the decision lands on people: was the handover stated clearly, did the person held responsible get a chance to explain. Both stretches affect the quality of execution, and missing either drops the chain at the execution level.

There is one action that can be put into practice: after each handling, the shift's record-keeper adds a line — which clause of the documentation was relied on, who signed, at what time it was reported. A month later, if most lines say "no basis", what needs changing is the process and the authority, not one side's attitude. Delivery pressure and communication arrangements cannot substitute for a safety criterion.

### A friend wants to move from the line to maintenance

(Fictional scene.) A friend has spent eight years on the assembly line and says they want to learn equipment maintenance, and asks both for an opinion. Either person could ask which maintenance tasks the friend wants to learn or suggest arranging authorised job shadowing to see what those tasks involve.

This is not about who is more realistic. The one pushing a trial fears three more years of standing still; the one asking about motive fears the friend changes posts only to discover they were tired. A workable move puts both in the same weekend: arrange a short observation session through the employer, then in the evening write three lines each for "what I have had enough of" and "what I want to learn".

The counterexamples stay too: ESTP will also ask first whether the family can carry the apprentice wage; INFP will also simply book the mentor. Agree a checkpoint — two weeks later, do not ask "have you decided", ask "did anything get done these two days".

### The supervisor says keep production running and repair on the late shift

(Fictional scene.) The instruction comes down, and neither will pretend not to have heard it, but the first thing to act on may differ. State the boundary first: a supervisor's production requirement cannot replace a safety criterion; when the equipment state is unclear, or the procedure does not allow continued running, report through the site process and let qualified people decide whether to stop. That has nothing to do with type.

In this fictional scene both hold the same authority. One approach asks the running conditions and monitoring in detail: which permitted modes the documentation allows, whether inspection should be tightened, when the spare part arrives. The other asks the human arrangements in detail: how many are on the late shift, who can handle it, who speaks outward if something deviates, whether the customer should be told in advance. Both bring the decision down to an executable level. Both types can combine these bases; which step is taken depends on the division of work, the authority and the information available.

The condition for changing the order is clear as well: where the procedure does not permit continued running, both arrangements give way to the safety conclusion; if only a newcomer is available, report the staffing limit through the site process so authorised staff can assess it. Which comes first depends on the procedure, the authority and who is present, not on type.
compare_blocks.title: Illustrative scenarios

compare_blocks.body:
Reading ESTP as reckless is the commonest shortcut. What lets them judge on the floor is confidence that the information they hold lines up; with too little, they will also step back, ask people and open the documentation. Willingness to act is also bounded by authority — without it, they can only report.

Reading INFP as overthinking and unable to take responsibility does not hold either. Holding back an opinion is often because the part of the cost others cannot see has been counted in: a crew blamed, a newcomer scolded. Put that cost on the table and a conclusion may come quickly; where the procedure is clear, they will also stop the line and report at once.

The third misread is using "equipment first or people first" as a typing basis. A person's account is itself information, and readings also need people to interpret them; the same type changes the choice with a different post and a different authority.

The fourth is taking a post for a type. Maintenance and planning posts shape how people speak, but are not decided by type; nor does it follow that one type is better suited to the floor — that turns a preference into a rank of ability.

body: Reading ESTP as reckless is the commonest shortcut. What lets them judge on the floor is confidence that the information they hold lines up; with too little, they will also step back, ask people and open the documentation. Willingness to act is also bounded by authority — without it, they can only report.

Reading INFP as overthinking and unable to take responsibility does not hold either. Holding back an opinion is often because the part of the cost others cannot see has been counted in: a crew blamed, a newcomer scolded. Put that cost on the table and a conclusion may come quickly; where the procedure is clear, they will also stop the line and report at once.

The third misread is using "equipment first or people first" as a typing basis. A person's account is itself information, and readings also need people to interpret them; the same type changes the choice with a different post and a different authority.

The fourth is taking a post for a type. Maintenance and planning posts shape how people speak, but are not decided by type; nor does it follow that one type is better suited to the floor — that turns a preference into a rank of ability.

Reading ESTP as reckless is the commonest shortcut. body: Only P is shared. E/I, S/N and T/F each describes a separate difference.

The shared P is easily read as "neither likes being managed by process", which mistakes outward stance for discipline. P says only that, facing the outer world, both more often take information in and leave room to adjust; how an inspection sheet is filled, how a shift is handed over, how detailed a record is — those follow the post and the procedure, and either type can be strict about them. If the resemblance stops at "neither follows process", every later comparison is bent out of shape.

The differences are read on all three axes at once: whether sourcing trusts checkable facts and past experience, or notices connections and possibility faster; whether the weighing relies on criteria that can be applied consistently, or counts people and costs in; and whether attention turns outward to the floor or inward for a first pass of one's own. All three coexist; the difference is which is relied on more often.
### Gearbox noise on the night shift: the same information, two weighings

In this fictional night-shift example, two workers hear the same unusual gearbox noise and have access to the same records. They have the same reporting duty and authority. Abnormal equipment noise is an abnormal condition: report it under site procedure first, and let qualified, authorised people decide from the equipment documentation and the procedure whether it can keep running — that applies to both, and neither may decide from a type to open the unit or relax a condition. What follows looks only at which information each may attend to, and how the basis is stated.

One approach emphasises confirmed observations in the existing records, such as the time the sound was heard and the last service date. That illustrates Sensing. Separately, asking whether the same reporting criterion applies across comparable shifts illustrates Thinking.

Another approach looks for a pattern across the same shift records or considers more than one explanation for what was reported. That illustrates Intuition. Separately, weighing how the handover affects the next crew illustrates Feeling. Either worker could use all four perspectives without changing the reporting procedure.

The costs sit on either side. Someone whose attention goes to the readings faster may underestimate communication lag: the information is still in one person's hands while others carry on the old way. Someone whose attention goes to people earlier may be caught by "who will be blamed" before the equipment state is clear, and the report may omit a detail that the next shift needs. Neither cost is about preference; both depend on the information, duty and deadline of the moment.

Keep the counterexamples. ESTP will open the documentation and call a qualified person when the equipment is unfamiliar; INFP will shout stop and report the moment someone moves toward a running part. The fork is not who moves first but which kind of basis is cited more often from the same information; sequence is not a criterion.
### Why not one function name overlaps

In the four-function notation used here, ESTP is Se–Ti–Fe–Ni and INFP is Fi–Ne–Si–Te. Side by side nothing shares a name: on the perceiving side Se and Ni against Ne and Si; on the judging side Ti and Fe against Fi and Te.

More precisely, the two share no function with the same name and attitude; each has perceiving and judging processes, but the processes in the dominant and auxiliary positions, and their directions, differ. ESTP's dominant faces outward and stays close to the facts at hand; INFP's dominant faces inward and stays close to the values they hold. That does not mean one has more or fewer mental operations than the other.

Function positions are the model's description of preference; they cannot be read as a sequence of actions, and they are not a list of strengths. Using them to infer whether two people work well together, or who attracts whom, goes beyond what this writing can support.

The attitude of the third position is not consistent across tables: for ESTP's Fe and INFP's Si, some writings mark an explicit attitude and some give only the function name. The disagreement does not change the first two positions; when reading a stack, check which set it declares. Both base descriptions are the [ESTP profile](/en/personality/estp) and the [INFP profile](/en/personality/infp).

body: The premise is aligned conditions: the same equipment, the same records, the same authority and deadline. If one is the shift owner and the other merely passing by, duty will cover both columns, with no relation to type.

Each row gives the same scene, the same information and the same constraints, states the basis each may attend to, and notes which axis it illustrates. Both types can use the other's approach; the table records only which is taken first more often, not who is right.

| The same scene (one set of information, the same constraints) | ESTP: the basis more likely attended to | INFP: the basis more likely attended to | What this row illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A noise record arrives | Whether readings, timestamps and the last service line up, and which items are confirmed | Why the accounts differ, and whether the same clue repeats across shifts | Sourcing preference, leaning S/N |

| When the two opinions conflict | Which criterion applies to everyone equally, and whether it can be written in advance | Where this conclusion lands on a specific crew and person, and whether that cost was counted | Basis for judgement, leaning T/F |

(Fictional scene.) The threshold is not set by a type. A month later, if most lines say "no basis", what needs changing is the process and the authority, not one side's attitude. Delivery pressure and communication arrangements cannot substitute for a safety criterion.

body: When results disagree, check the item bank name, version, language and scoring convention first, then which kind of experience you were referring to: being responsible for handling on site, or explaining the consequences of handling. Change the position and the answer often changes with it; that looks more like the effect of the answering situation than a change of preference.

Writing "why I trusted it" is more useful than "what I did first" — the same choice to look at readings first may rest on "the procedure requires confirming first" or on "readings persuade people best", and the two point at different things.

sections.title: Quick answer

sections.body_md:
Only P is shared. E/I, S/N and T/F each describes a separate difference.

The shared P is easily read as "neither likes being managed by process", which mistakes outward stance for discipline. P says only that, facing the outer world, both more often take information in and leave room to adjust; how an inspection sheet is filled, how a shift is handed over, how detailed a record is — those follow the post and the procedure, and either type can be strict about them. If the resemblance stops at "neither follows process", every later comparison is bent out of shape.

The differences are read on all three axes at once: whether sourcing trusts checkable facts and past experience, or notices connections and possibility faster; whether the weighing relies on criteria that can be applied consistently, or counts people and costs in; and whether attention turns outward to the floor or inward for a first pass of one's own. All three coexist; the difference is which is relied on more often.

### Gearbox noise on the night shift: the same information, two weighings

In this fictional night-shift example, two workers hear the same unusual gearbox noise and have access to the same records. They have the same reporting duty and authority. Abnormal equipment noise is an abnormal condition: report it under site procedure first, and let qualified, authorised people decide from the equipment documentation and the procedure whether it can keep running — that applies to both, and neither may decide from a type to open the unit or relax a condition. What follows looks only at which information each may attend to, and how the basis is stated.

One approach emphasises confirmed observations in the existing records, such as the time the sound was heard and the last service date. That illustrates Sensing. Separately, asking whether the same reporting criterion applies across comparable shifts illustrates Thinking.

Another approach looks for a pattern across the same shift records or considers more than one explanation for what was reported. That illustrates Intuition. Separately, weighing how the handover affects the next crew illustrates Feeling. Either worker could use all four perspectives without changing the reporting procedure.

The costs sit on either side. Someone whose attention goes to the readings faster may underestimate communication lag: the information is still in one person's hands while others carry on the old way. Someone whose attention goes to people earlier may be caught by "who will be blamed" before the equipment state is clear, and the report may omit a detail that the next shift needs. Neither cost is about preference; both depend on the information, duty and deadline of the moment.

Keep the counterexamples. ESTP will open the documentation and call a qualified person when the equipment is unfamiliar; INFP will shout stop and report the moment someone moves toward a running part. The fork is not who moves first but which kind of basis is cited more often from the same information; sequence is not a criterion.

### Why not one function name overlaps

In the four-function notation used here, ESTP is Se–Ti–Fe–Ni and INFP is Fi–Ne–Si–Te. Side by side nothing shares a name: on the perceiving side Se and Ni against Ne and Si; on the judging side Ti and Fe against Fi and Te.

More precisely, the two share no function with the same name and attitude; each has perceiving and judging processes, but the processes in the dominant and auxiliary positions, and their directions, differ. ESTP's dominant faces outward and stays close to the facts at hand; INFP's dominant faces inward and stays close to the values they hold. That does not mean one has more or fewer mental operations than the other.

Function positions are the model's description of preference; they cannot be read as a sequence of actions, and they are not a list of strengths. Using them to infer whether two people work well together, or who attracts whom, goes beyond what this writing can support.

The attitude of the third position is not consistent across tables: for ESTP's Fe and INFP's Si, some writings mark an explicit attitude and some give only the function name. The disagreement does not change the first two positions; when reading a stack, check which set it declares. Both base descriptions are the [ESTP profile](/en/personality/estp) and the [INFP profile](/en/personality/infp).

sections.body_md:
The premise is aligned conditions: the same equipment, the same records, the same authority and deadline. If one is the shift owner and the other merely passing by, duty will cover both columns, with no relation to type.

Each row gives the same scene, the same information and the same constraints, states the basis each may attend to, and notes which axis it illustrates. Both types can use the other's approach; the table records only which is taken first more often, not who is right.

| The same scene (one set of information, the same constraints) | ESTP: the basis more likely attended to | INFP: the basis more likely attended to | What this row illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A noise record arrives | Whether readings, timestamps and the last service line up, and which items are confirmed | Why the accounts differ, and whether the same clue repeats across shifts | Sourcing preference, leaning S/N |
| Judging what the symptom points at | Compare item by item against known component behaviour, and see which fact matches | Join several scattered items and see whether they point at one possibility | Sourcing preference, leaning S/N |
| When the two opinions conflict | Which criterion applies to everyone equally, and whether it can be written in advance | Where this conclusion lands on a specific crew and person, and whether that cost was counted | Basis for judgement, leaning T/F |
| Writing the review afterwards | Weigh whether the same documented deviations meet the agreed handover criteria | Weigh what those same deviations mean for the people taking over | Basis for judgement, leaning T/F |
| Where attention goes when the discussion stalls | May make sense of the same known information by discussing it with those present | May make sense of the same known information through private reflection | Direction of attention, leaning E/I |
| Following the same machine for several days | May clarify what the same recorded changes mean by discussing them with the team | May clarify what the same recorded changes mean by reflecting on them privately | Direction of attention, leaning E/I |

The differences in the table are not a scale of ability. An ESTP who has just changed posts may only stand and watch, and an INFP who has run shifts for years may report everything the procedure requires first; duty, experience, authority and information all rewrite performance.
sections.title: ESTP and INFP in one minute

sections.body_md:
Scope note: the three passages below are editorial fictions about ordinary situations, covering the organisation of information and communication only, not equipment handling procedure. Noise, temperature, vibration and fitness to continue running are equipment and safety judgements, decided by qualified, authorised people under the equipment documentation and site procedure; what the two can do is state clearly what they saw and heard, report through the process, and make the handover and the human impact clear. In an emergency, seek help first and act on site and professional guidance.

### After the noise: who sets the threshold, how communication is arranged

(Fictional scene.) The threshold is not set by a type. Temperature limits, vibration limits and the permitted ways to run come from the manufacturer's documentation and site procedure, signed off by qualified and authorised people. When neither is in that role, what they can do is record the symptom, the timestamp and the report already made, and mark clearly in the handover what has no conclusion yet.

On that basis, each may watch a different stretch. ESTP more often watches whether the criterion is applied consistently: is this the same standard as last time, has anyone relaxed it on experience. INFP more often watches how the decision lands on people: was the handover stated clearly, did the person held responsible get a chance to explain. Both stretches affect the quality of execution, and missing either drops the chain at the execution level.

There is one action that can be put into practice: after each handling, the shift's record-keeper adds a line — which clause of the documentation was relied on, who signed, at what time it was reported. A month later, if most lines say "no basis", what needs changing is the process and the authority, not one side's attitude. Delivery pressure and communication arrangements cannot substitute for a safety criterion.

### A friend wants to move from the line to maintenance

(Fictional scene.) A friend has spent eight years on the assembly line and says they want to learn equipment maintenance, and asks both for an opinion. Either person could ask which maintenance tasks the friend wants to learn or suggest arranging authorised job shadowing to see what those tasks involve.

This is not about who is more realistic. The one pushing a trial fears three more years of standing still; the one asking about motive fears the friend changes posts only to discover they were tired. A workable move puts both in the same weekend: arrange a short observation session through the employer, then in the evening write three lines each for "what I have had enough of" and "what I want to learn".

The counterexamples stay too: ESTP will also ask first whether the family can carry the apprentice wage; INFP will also simply book the mentor. Agree a checkpoint — two weeks later, do not ask "have you decided", ask "did anything get done these two days".

### The supervisor says keep production running and repair on the late shift

(Fictional scene.) The instruction comes down, and neither will pretend not to have heard it, but the first thing to act on may differ. State the boundary first: a supervisor's production requirement cannot replace a safety criterion; when the equipment state is unclear, or the procedure does not allow continued running, report through the site process and let qualified people decide whether to stop. That has nothing to do with type.

In this fictional scene both hold the same authority. One approach asks the running conditions and monitoring in detail: which permitted modes the documentation allows, whether inspection should be tightened, when the spare part arrives. The other asks the human arrangements in detail: how many are on the late shift, who can handle it, who speaks outward if something deviates, whether the customer should be told in advance. Both bring the decision down to an executable level. Both types can combine these bases; which step is taken depends on the division of work, the authority and the information available.

The condition for changing the order is clear as well: where the procedure does not permit continued running, both arrangements give way to the safety conclusion; if only a newcomer is available, report the staffing limit through the site process so authorised staff can assess it. Which comes first depends on the procedure, the authority and who is present, not on type.
sections.title: ESTP and INFP at work and in relationships

sections.body_md:
Reading ESTP as reckless is the commonest shortcut. What lets them judge on the floor is confidence that the information they hold lines up; with too little, they will also step back, ask people and open the documentation. Willingness to act is also bounded by authority — without it, they can only report.

Reading INFP as overthinking and unable to take responsibility does not hold either. Holding back an opinion is often because the part of the cost others cannot see has been counted in: a crew blamed, a newcomer scolded. Put that cost on the table and a conclusion may come quickly; where the procedure is clear, they will also stop the line and report at once.

The third misread is using "equipment first or people first" as a typing basis. A person's account is itself information, and readings also need people to interpret them; the same type changes the choice with a different post and a different authority.

The fourth is taking a post for a type. Maintenance and planning posts shape how people speak, but are not decided by type; nor does it follow that one type is better suited to the floor — that turns a preference into a rank of ability.
sections.title: ESTP and INFP: avoiding misreads

sections.body_md:
When results disagree, check the item bank name, version, language and scoring convention first, then which kind of experience you were referring to: being responsible for handling on site, or explaining the consequences of handling. Change the position and the answer often changes with it; that looks more like the effect of the answering situation than a change of preference.

Do not catch a single reaction. Take three recent incidents, sudden or half-sudden, and write three lines for each: what the post required and what authority you held, which information or standard you trusted, and whether you would still prefer the same line of thinking in another setting. Writing "why I trusted it" is more useful than "what I did first" — the same choice to look at readings first may rest on "the procedure requires confirming first" or on "readings persuade people best", and the two point at different things.

Rich entries in both columns are common, and only show that both kinds of information deserved attention in those situations; they do not show that a questionnaire score sits near a boundary. Only when the tool explicitly reports dimension scores or preference clarity should a borderline result be interpreted by that tool's notes; retesting in another setting can serve as a check, but a new result cannot rule on which type you are.

items.answer:
Because this pair differs on three of the four preference pairs — E/I, S/N and T/F all differ — which makes it useful for keeping the three axes apart instead of merging them into "one acts, one thinks about people".

P is often read as "neither follows process and neither likes meetings", which mistakes outward stance for discipline. P means taking information in and keeping room to adjust when facing the outer world; how records are kept and how shifts are handed over follow the post and the procedure, and either type can be very detailed. The real differences return to sourcing, the basis for judgement and the direction of attention.
items.question: They share only P — why compare them at all?

items.answer:
No. Different names only mean the two have no overlapping process at the four positions; they do not mean either lacks a kind of mental operation.

In the four-function notation used here, ESTP is Se–Ti–Fe–Ni and INFP is Fi–Ne–Si–Te: ESTP's dominant faces outward and stays close to the facts at hand, INFP's faces inward and stays close to the values they hold; both have perceiving and judging processes. Function positions describe emphasis in preference, not a list of abilities, and do not predict the order of actions.
items.question: With no shared function name, is there nothing in common?

items.answer:
Both will. Whether to stop and who stops belongs to site safety and authority, decided by procedure and by qualified people; either type may shout stop and report at once in front of obvious danger.

The difference is not speed but which kind of basis is cited more from the same information: which information is emphasised (S/N) and which criteria are weighed (T/F). Either person can use the same records and consider the people affected. Who reports afterwards and who stays for the handover also follows the shift's division of duty, not type.
items.question: INFP will also demand a stop on the spot, and ESTP will also consider people first?

items.answer:
Both attend to equipment and to people; the difference is which is taken first more often: whether the symptom can be mapped to a specific part and the criterion applied consistently, or whether the accounts line up and who the conclusion will land on.

Both kinds of information affect the quality of communication: without the first, the report cannot state the symptom; without the second, the cost is discovered later, on someone who never spoke. But organising information is not the handling decision — whether the machine may keep running and whether it needs repair is decided by qualified, authorised people under the documentation and the procedure.
items.question: Handling an equipment anomaly, what may each attend to first?

items.answer:
Two misreadings dominate: one side feels the other "is always worrying about people and never says how the equipment actually is", and the other feels the first "only cares about the machine, not the people".

Both readings miss half. A workable move is to speak in two parts: first the confirmed symptoms and criterion, then what the decision means for the people involved, without treating the other part as noise. In an argument, ask first "who would this decision hurt most if it goes wrong", then return to "which basis can go into the record".
items.question: Living or working together, what do they most often misread in each other?

items.answer:
Separate preference from situation first, then look at what the items actually ask.

People who handle incidents for years develop fast on-site judgement, and people who own delivery dates and staffing for years develop the habit of counting the human side first; those are the results of job training. Items asking whether someone likes risk or often reflects on themselves also easily read a habit as a preference. To check, take the same tool in two different situations and record the post and the experience you referred to; the results are for reference, not for fixing a type on yourself.
